lines: Jordan Rivera
+1 (555) 010-2287 | jordan.rivera@example.com | example.com/in/jrivera
Date of birth: 22 May 1997 | Nationality: Chilean
EDUCATION
Northgate University | M.P.H. in Biostatistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2019 - May 2021
EXPERIENCE
Meridian Heart Institute | Clinical Research Coordinator | Metro City, USA | Sep 2022 - Jul 2025
- Coordinated a 3-site randomized trial of a nurse-led discharge program for 640 heart-failure patients, finishing enrollment 4 months early with 94% of follow-up visits completed.
- Cut data-entry errors in the trial database from 6.1% to 1.8% of fields by adding range checks and double entry for the primary outcome.
- Estimated median survival in each arm by averaging the follow-up time of patients who died, excluding censored patients.
- Reconciling adverse-event reports across three sites, coding them to MedDRA terms and cross-checking them against pharmacy records each week, cut unresolved safety queries from 45 to 6.
- Presented monthly safety reports to the data monitoring committee, and all 4 reviews passed without a protocol change.
- Trained 9 site nurses on the consent process and outcome forms, and no consent deviations were found at the final audit.
Northgate University Hospital | Research Assistant | Metro City, USA | Apr 2022 - Aug 2022
- Randomized patients by assigning those admitted on odd-numbered days to the program and even-numbered days to usual care.
- Interviewed 25 patients about missed clinic visits; the findings added text reminders that cut no-shows from 18% to 11%.
- Wrote the study's data dictionary for 180 variables, which the next two cohort studies reused.

- Cleaned and merged lab data from two hospital systems while also scheduling participant visits, ordering study supplies, taking minutes at lab meetings and covering the front desk, which resolved 1,200 mismatched patient identifiers.
PROJECTS
Asthma Readmission Analysis | Independent Project | R | Jan 2025 - Present
- Harnessed cutting-edge analytics to deliver transformative, patient-centered insights into respiratory health outcomes.
- Found that 7-day follow-up cut readmission from 12% to 8%, a 50% reduction, after adjusting for age and insurance.
- Raised the survey response rate by 20% with SMS reminders, from 35% to 55% of invited residents.
Community Health Survey | Volunteer, Team of 5 | REDCap | Mar 2020 - Aug 2020
- Designed a 30-question community health survey and collected 1,100 responses, giving the clinic its first estimate of uninsured residents by neighborhood.
- The survey was translated into Spanish and piloted with 20 residents before launch.
- Wrote the survey's data codebook, which the clinic used for its follow-up survey the next year.
SKILLS
Tools: R, REDCap
Methods: randomized trials, regression, mixed-effects models, survey design

items.says: Make sure the LinkedIn URL is complete and clickable in the submitted PDF.
items.because: Reviewers should be able to use the link.

items.says: Add a city or region if useful for the roles you are targeting.
Remove the date of birth.
items.because: It is not needed to evaluate your qualifications and may invite age-related bias.

items.says: Remove nationality unless an application asks for it or it is relevant to work authorization.
items.because: If work authorization matters, state that directly instead.

items.says: Consider placing Education after Experience and Skills.
items.because: You have several years of relevant work history.

items.says: Add undergraduate education if it is relevant or helps complete your education history.
items.because: Omitting it could be confusing.

items.says: Make location, date, punctuation, and bullet formatting consistent.
items.because: Consistency improves scanning.

items.says: Clarify your specific contribution to the three-site trial.
items.because: It would show what you did.

items.says: Define what “94% of follow-up visits completed” measures.
items.because: A denominator or measurement period would help readers interpret the metric.

items.says: Clarify how the data-entry error rate was measured.
items.because: The before-and-after rates need to be explainable.

items.says: The stated method does not validly estimate median survival.
items.because: Survival estimates must account for censored patients, typically with a method such as Kaplan–Meier.

items.says: Change “Reconciling” to match the past tense of the role.
Remove the manual line break splitting a word.
items.because: The document should wrap naturally.

items.says: Clarify the period and definition of unresolved safety queries.
items.because: Those details explain the reduction from 45 to 6.

items.says: Be precise about your role and what the four reviews' outcome signifies.
items.because: The wording could imply that your work made protocol changes unnecessary.

items.says: Clarify the scope of the audit behind “no consent deviations.”
items.because: The finding may apply only to records reviewed, not the entire study.

items.says: Do not call odd/even-day assignment randomized allocation.
items.because: Admission-day assignment is predictable, can introduce selection bias, and is not equivalent to randomization.

items.says: Clarify when and over what period the drop in no-shows was measured.
items.because: It is unclear whether the 18%-to-11% reduction followed the reminders.

items.says: Explain the data dictionary's role in enabling the later studies if known.
items.because: That would make your contribution clearer.

items.says: Separate or prioritize the data-cleaning achievement and trim unrelated routine duties.
items.because: Combining them makes the identifier-resolution result hard to connect to your work.

items.says: Explain what resolving 1,200 mismatched identifiers means and how you contributed.
Distinguish completed work from remaining work if that matters to the role.
items.because: The project is ongoing.

items.says: Remove the “cutting-edge analytics” bullet.
items.because: It is vague and promotional and says nothing about the analysis, method, or findings.

items.says: Correct the claimed 50% readmission reduction.
items.because: A drop from 12% to 8% is 4 percentage points, or about a 33% relative reduction.

items.says: Avoid saying follow-up “cut” readmissions unless the design supports a causal conclusion.
items.because: Otherwise, the result should be described as an association or observed difference.

items.says: Include sample size and uncertainty measures if available.
items.because: They would make the result easier to assess.

items.says: Explain the design, comparison groups, model, and important limitations.
items.because: Adjustment for age and insurance alone may not address confounding.

items.says: Correct the claim of a 20% response-rate increase.
items.because: A rise from 35% to 55% is a 20-percentage-point increase.

items.says: Clarify whether the survey is part of the readmission analysis or a separate outcome.
items.because: Their relationship is unclear in the current project description.

items.says: Clarify whether the 1,100 responses were complete.
Clarify whether the neighborhood estimates came from a representative sample.
items.because: Otherwise, the estimates may need to be interpreted cautiously.

items.says: Clarify whether translation and piloting were substantive parts of your contribution.
Avoid implying the pilot of 20 residents establishes broad validity.
Specify your individual contribution to the codebook if “wrote” overstates a team effort.
Add other tools you can use confidently, if applicable.
items.because: The tools list may be too sparse for biostatistics roles.

items.says: List only methods you have actually applied.
items.because: Methods based only on coursework or brief exposure should not be listed.

items.says: Consider naming specific analyses or study-design methods relevant to target roles.
Group tools and methods consistently, and add relevant clinical-research competencies or certifications if you have them.
Tailor the methods and achievements to each target role.
items.because: Biostatistician, clinical research, and data-analysis positions call for different emphasis.
